 Why don’t Americans celebrate International Workers’ Day on May 1? [...] ## How the Date Is Decided

The rule is short enough to memorize: the first Monday in September. No equinox math, no lunar calculation, no church table. Find the first day of September on a calendar, count forward to the next Monday, and that is Labor Day. If September 1 is itself a Monday, that is the holiday. results.title: Labour Day - Wikipedia
results.content: The 1st of May, or first Monday in May, is a national public holiday in many countries, in most cases known as "International Workers' Day" or a similar name. Some countries celebrate a Labour Day on other dates significant to them, such as the United States and Canada, which celebrate Labor Day "Labor Day (United States)") on the first Monday of September. In 1955, the Catholic Church dedicated 1 May to "Saint Joseph the Worker". Replacing another feast of St. Joseph, this date was chosen by [...] is an official public holiday in many countries. In most countries, Labour Day is synonymous with, or linked with, International Workers' Day, which happens on 1 May. It was originally chosen to commemorate the 1886 general strike which culminated in the Haymarket affair. In the United States "Labor Day (United States)") and in Canada "Labour Day (Canada)"), it is a public holiday on the first Monday in September. [...] In the United States and Canada, a September holiday, called Labor or Labour Day, was first proposed in the 1880s. In 1882, Matthew Maguire "Matthew Maguire (labor activist)"), a machinist, first proposed a Labor Day holiday on the first Monday of September while serving as secretary of the Central Labor Union (CLU) of New York. # History of Labor Day

ILGWU Local 62 marches in a Labor Day parade. Source: 

ILGWU Local 62 marches in a Labor Day parade. Source: 

Observed the first Monday in September, Labor Day is an annual celebration of the social and economic achievements of American workers. The holiday is rooted in the late nineteenth century, when labor activists pushed for a federal holiday to recognize the many contributions workers have made to America’s strength, prosperity, and well-being. [...] The first Labor Day holiday was celebrated on Tuesday, September 5, 1882, in New York City, in accordance with the plans of the Central Labor Union. The Central Labor Union held its second Labor Day holiday just a year later, on September 5, 1883.

By 1894, 23 more states had adopted the holiday, and on June 28, 1894, President Grover Cleveland signed a law making the first Monday in September of each year a national holiday.
